title: Your spouse or closest person
tomorrow: why would Jesus tell grown-ups to become like children?

lines: A FRIEND FALLS IN LOVE AND VANISHES.
DOES ONE LOVE SHRINK THE HEART?
cards: A friend falls in love and disappears. The group chat goes quiet, Friday plans stop, and when you do see them, every story is about one person.
So here's a fair question: can loving one person deeply make your heart smaller? Inside the Catholic tradition, two honest answers sit side by side. Paul gives one.
The Church's teaching on marriage gives another. Neither one is a rule for your love life. Let each of them make its case, in its own words, and see which part of each you can't quite argue with.

teach.b: Paul first, writing to the Christians in Corinth. Marrying is no sin, he says plainly.
But the unmarried can give themselves to the things of the Lord, while the married man is busy with how to please his wife, "and he is divided."
Paul's worry isn't that love is bad. It's that one love can crowd out the others.
The tradition has honored that view: priests, sisters and brothers who stay unmarried so their love can stay wide, open to anyone who knocks. Now the other side.

The Church calls marriage a sacrament, and the Catechism says husband and wife help each other toward holiness, in the ordinary grind of a shared life. On this view, one close love doesn't shrink the heart. It trains it.
You learn patience on the person who leaves the dishes.
You learn forgiveness on the one who knows exactly how to hurt you. And here's the surprise to tell a friend: the Catechism refuses to pick a winner.
It says honoring the unmarried life for God's kingdom and the Christian understanding of marriage go together, and each one supports the other.
What both sides share is this: love is a choice, made again and again. The wedding vows promise it in good times and in bad. You don't choose once.
You choose again on an ordinary Tuesday.

how: Catholics marry in a sacrament, promising faithfulness in good times and in bad; others, like priests and religious sisters and brothers, stay unmarried for the kingdom of God, and the Church honors both.

games.q: what does “your spouse or closest person” mean?
o: the person you're required to obey before all others
the one love you choose again and again, every day
whoever you happen to spend the most time with

games.q: two honest answers — tap the pairs.
p: spouses help each other to holiness

s: Paul says getting married is a sin
he says plainly that marrying is no sin; his worry is a divided heart.
the Catechism ranks the unmarried life above marriage
it says the two go together, and each supports the other.
in Catholic teaching, spouses help each other toward holiness
the Catechism says so: the shared life itself is the road.

games.q: your friend is thinking about becoming a sister and says marriage would split her heart. what's the best case for her side?
o: Paul: the unmarried can give their whole selves to the Lord, and their love stays wide.
Paul taught that marriage is a sin, so she's avoiding one.
the Church says unmarried people love more than married people.
games.why: the strongest form of her view is Paul's own: an undivided heart, open to anyone. the Church honors it, and honors marriage too, without ranking them.

practice: Bring to mind the person closest to you: a spouse, a best friend, a parent, a sibling. Walk through their day tomorrow in your mind, hour by hour.
Find one small thing you could do for them that they won't ask for, and if you have paper nearby, write it down by hand.

wordCard.voice: Your spouse or closest person. The one love you choose again every day, which can widen the heart instead of shrinking it. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, Paul's word in his letter to Corinth: he is divided.

carryVoice: Your line: chosen again. Not once, at the start, but in the dishes and the bad days too. Until tomorrow.
